hook.line: Everyone has lost their keys and sworn they left them on the table. Spanish has a polite way to say "I'm sure, but I can't prove it", so you are not caught out when the keys turn up in your coat.
hook.es: Juraría que dejé las llaves en la mesa.
hook.en: I could swear I left the keys on the table.

examples.es: Juraría que dejé las llaves en la mesa.
examples.en: I could swear I left the keys on the table.

examples.es: Sospecho que Altamira ya compró el edificio.
examples.en: I suspect Altamira has already bought the building.

examples.es: Me da la impresión de que Tomás no quiere vender.
examples.en: I get the impression that Tomás doesn't want to sell.

examples.es: Juraría que Hernando estuvo aquí esta mañana.
examples.en: I could swear Hernando was here this morning.

examples.es: Sospechamos que el senador sabe más.
examples.en: We suspect the senator knows more.

examples.es: Me da la impresión de que ellos están nerviosos.
examples.en: I get the impression that they are nervous.

rule:
*Juraría que* is "I could swear that": you feel sure, but you cannot prove it, and you may be wrong. *Sospecho que* is "I suspect that", usually about something bad. *Me da la impresión de que* is "I get the impression that".

After all three the verb stays plain: *dejé*, *compró*, *quiere*.

The *-ía* ending is the "would" form. Spanish says "I would swear" where English says "I could swear". Compare *me consta*: that one has proof, while these three run on gut feeling.
smallPrint: Teachers call these verbs of subjective certainty, and the verb after them takes the indicative.

readAndPick.es: Juraría que dejé las llaves en la mesa.
options: I could swear I will leave the keys on the table.
I could swear I left the keys on the table.
I could swear you left the keys on the table.

readAndPick.es: Sospechamos que el senador sabe más.
options: I suspect the senator knows more.
They suspect the senator knows more.
We suspect the senator knows more.

readAndPick.es: Me da la impresión de que Tomás no quiere vender.
options: I get the impression that Tomás doesn't want to sell.
Tomás gets the impression that I don't want to sell.
I get the impression that Tomás didn't want to sell.

readAndPick.es: Juraría que Hernando estuvo aquí esta mañana.
options: I could swear Hernando will be here this morning.
I could swear Hernando is here this morning.
I could swear Hernando was here this morning.

readAndPick.es: Sospecho que Altamira ya compró el edificio.
options: I suspect Altamira will buy the building.
I suspect Altamira has already bought the building.
I suspect Altamira is buying the building.

readAndPick.es: Juraría que Vale estaba en la cocina.
options: I could swear Vale was in the kitchen.
I could swear Vale is in the kitchen.
I could swear Vale will be in the kitchen.

readAndPick.es: Me da la impresión de que ellos están nerviosos.
options: I get the impression that we are nervous.
They get the impression that I am nervous.
I get the impression that they are nervous.

readAndPick.es: Sospecho que no tienen el permiso.
options: I suspect I don't have the permit.
I suspect they didn't have the permit.
I suspect they don't have the permit.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick and type the whole sentence: *Juraría que ___ las llaves en la mesa.* (*dejé* or *dejaría*) I could swear I left the keys on the table.
yourTurn.answer: Juraría que dejé las llaves en la mesa.
yourTurn.why: *Juraría* already carries the "would"; the thing you left is a plain past: *dejé*.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick and type the whole sentence: *Me da la impresión de que Tomás ___ vender.* (*no quiere* or *no quiera*) I get the impression that Tomás doesn't want to sell.
yourTurn.answer: Me da la impresión de que Tomás no quiere vender.
yourTurn.why: An impression is something you take as true, so the verb stays plain: *no quiere*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: I could swear Hernando was here this morning.
yourTurn.answer: Juraría que Hernando estuvo aquí esta mañana.
accept: Juraría que Hernando estuvo esta mañana aquí.
yourTurn.why: *Estuvo* is a plain past after *juraría que*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: I suspect Altamira has already bought the building.
yourTurn.answer: Sospecho que Altamira ya compró el edificio.
accept: Sospecho que Altamira compró ya el edificio.
yourTurn.why: *Sospecho que* opens the guess, and the rest is an ordinary statement.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: We suspect the senator knows more.
yourTurn.answer: Sospechamos que el senador sabe más.
yourTurn.why: *Sospechamos* is the "we" form, and *sabe* stays plain.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it negative: *Juraría que Vale estaba en la cocina.* (I could swear Vale was not in the kitchen)
yourTurn.answer: Juraría que Vale no estaba en la cocina.
yourTurn.why: The *no* goes in front of the verb inside the statement, not in front of *juraría*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: I get the impression that they are nervous.
yourTurn.answer: Me da la impresión de que ellos están nerviosos.
accept: Me da la impresión de que están nerviosos.

pitfalls.wrong: Juraría que haya dejado las llaves en la mesa.
pitfalls.right: Juraría que dejé las llaves en la mesa.
pitfalls.why: Almost. You feel sure, so the verb after *juraría que* stays plain.

pitfalls.wrong: Juro que dejé las llaves en la mesa.
pitfalls.right: Juraría que dejé las llaves en la mesa.
pitfalls.why: Almost. *Juro* is a flat oath; *juraría* leaves room to be wrong, which is what you want here.

pitfalls.wrong: Me da la impresión que Tomás no quiere vender.
pitfalls.right: Me da la impresión de que Tomás no quiere vender.
pitfalls.why: Almost. After *impresión* Spanish keeps the *de* in front of *que*.

personal: Think of something you are sure about but cannot prove, like where you left something. Say it with *Juraría que*, then add one hunch about someone you know with *Sospecho que*.
